On the first day of AIE Code Summit, OpenAI showed how developers can steer Codex by voice, hand off work to the cloud, and make use of dots. AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here ,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” Codex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. model:vllm|title:warmctl fast cold start.content_excerpt: GPU checkpoint/restore for vLLM: snapshot a warmed-up engine (compiled kernels, CUDA graphs, weights, 1-8 GPUs) into an OCI image and restore it in seconds instead of a multi-minute cold start. Scale to zero, spot GPUs, Kubernetes optional. warmctl is GPU checkpoint/restore for vLLM. It snapshots a warmed-up engine and restores it in seconds on any host with the same GPUs and NVIDIA driver branch, so a new replica skips weight loading, torch.compile, kernel autotuning and CUDA graph capture. GLM-5.3-Flash on 8×H100: vLLM cold start 650 s, warmctl up 37 s, then stock serving speed. That makes scale to zero, fast autoscaling and spot GPU replacement practical for large models. The public catalog has 21 models on H100, H200, B200, B300, L40S and RTX PRO 6000. Any other model vLLM serves with sleep mode, build yourself ( tutorial ): warmctl up to serving, snapshot in page cache, against a vLLM cold start (weights on local disk, empty compile caches). ~ is the time to a ready engine while building the snapshot; where we measured both, a plain cold start was 1–24% shorter. On B200, GLM-5.3-Flash restores in 44 s (8×B200) and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in 73 s (4×B200). Every platform is in the catalog . GLM-5.3-Flash on 8×H100 by phase, from page cache and from a cold network file share (about 10 GB/s): Restored engines serve at stock vLLM speed or faster (GLM-5.3-Flash: 100–136% of stock throughput). build starts vLLM in a container, warms it over every shape in the profile and checkpoints the processes (CRIU), the GPUs (cuda-checkpoint) and the weights. push stores the snapshot as an OCI artifact, one per platform. up checks the host, restores everything at the same GPU addresses, runs a canary against the original engine and opens an OpenAI-compatible API. Multi-GPU engines keep NCCL and symmetric memory through NVIDIA cuInterpose. Details: how a restore works , architecture , shared GPU memory , registries and caches . warmctl is in beta: releases are GitHub pre-releases, and every user-facing change is in the CHANGELOG . Each restore is checked before it serves: the host must match the snapshot before anything is downloaded, every file carries its SHA-256, every weights allocation is compared by a GPU fingerprint, and a canary prompt must get the original engine's answer (bitwise for large models). story|title:agentguard transaction guard.content_excerpt: Transaction guardrails for AI agents that hold crypto wallets - simulate, evaluate against policy + reputation, allow/block/escalate with a signed audit trail. EVM + Solana AgentGuard is a transaction guardrail layer for AI agents that hold crypto wallets. Before an agent signs or broadcasts anything, it submits the proposed transaction to AgentGuard, which simulates it against live chain state, evaluates the simulated effects against an operator-defined policy, and returns allow , block or escalate with a human-readable explanation, a 0–100 risk score and an immutable audit record. Agents never get to decide for themselves whether a transaction is safe. It works on EVM chains and Solana, decodes the usual drain vectors (unlimited approvals, setApprovalForAll , permits, swaps with zero minimum output, SetAuthority, interactions with never-seen contracts), and ships with a conservative default policy plus a TypeScript SDK that wraps any signer so that signTransaction / sendTransaction are checked transparently. On top of the rule engine, a contract reputation layer ( @agentguard/reputation , in this repo) aggregates allow/deny lists, on-chain heuristics (age, proxy, bytecode size) and optional external intel feeds, and an optional behavioral anomaly layer ( @agentguard/behavior , separately licensed, see What's open and what's not ) scores each transaction against the agent's own learned baseline. Both plug into the same pipeline and both fail closed: an outage or an unreadable profile escalates, never allows. Everything in this repository is open source under the Apache License 2.0 : the shared types, the policy engine and default policy, the EVM and Solana simulation adapters, the contract reputation layer, the HTTP API with its tamper-evident audit log, the SDK, the demo and all of the tests. The behavioral anomaly layer is not in this repository. It ships as a separately licensed package, @agentguard/behavior , that learns a per-agent baseline (counterparties, amounts, cadence, approvals) from allowed decisions and flags transactions that are out of character for that agent, for example a $95 transfer to a never-paid address from an agent whose history is 30 routine $5 payments, which no static rule catches. It plugs into the open core without any code change here: The @agentguard/behavior package lives at https://github.com/Radmo3/agentguard-behavior (private; contact the maintainers for licensing). story|title:an ai agent said the code wa.content_excerpt: Agent A writes a change. Agent B reviews it and says it looks great. Agent A then edits one more file “real quick” and ships. Nobody lied. The review was fine. It was a review of different code. I have been doing this for roughly thirty years, and I can report that “the thing we checked is not the thing we shipped” is the oldest bug in the business. We have simply found a way to do it faster and with more confidence. I wrote Uncle ( github.com/unclehq/uncle ) because I got tired of it. At Yahoo I built Yahoo Mail's anti-spam system. Billions of messages a month, six patents, and one durable lesson: a component does not get to declare its own output trustworthy because it produced it. Spammers taught me that. Apparently it also applies to the thing we now let write our code, review our code, and then tell us how it went. Today's workflow: the agent implements, tests, reviews itself, and reports “done, all green.” Did the tests run? Did they finish? Did the reviewer look at the final code? Who knows, ask the agent. (It will say yes. It is very confident. It is always very confident.) A second reviewing agent does not fix this. Adding reviewers to an unbound review is just adding more people to a meeting that has already ended. A Git tree has a hash. That is a concrete thing to staple evidence to. So record that the review passed against a particular tree, that the tests passed against that same tree, that a human approved it, and then check, before publishing, that you are still holding that tree. Here is a real run from a demo project: The last green check is the one that matters here: the tree you are holding, 9edd…fedc , is the tree that was reviewed, so the evidence applies to this code. That is all it tells you. Two lines are red. The verification run failed (one command regressed against the baseline), and the adversarial-review gate was approved by the agent on nobody's behalf, because the run was unattended. Uncle prints both instead of rounding up. Also note the signature line: a signature is present, but with no trust root to check it against, it proves nothing about who signed. Verified , signed and a human looked at it are different claims, and the tool refuses to blur them. Revolutionary, I know. Change the tree and the evidence stops applying. The only twist is that the workflow has to enforce it, because “please remember to re-run the review” in a prompt is a wish, not a control. Same for the evidence itself. story|title:botpsy on device personal as.content_excerpt: Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information. story|title:codemm your coding agent wri.content_excerpt: Learn any language or framework one step at a time, with your own coding agent as the tutor. Codemm is an open-source app for learning to code by practice. Your own coding agent (Claude Code or Codex, with your own account) writes the lessons and exercises. Codemm checks each exercise against its tests, grades your code in a sandbox, and tracks what you've mastered. Codemm launches your agent; it never calls a model API, and it never reads, stores or asks for credentials. It ships no languages: your agent sets up each language or framework the first time you need it, and Codemm checks that it works. What counts. Try it is never recorded. Check records an attempt, except for a check of the unedited starter or one that failed for a reason outside your code (Docker stopped, for example). Mastery moves only on an exercise's first check, or when you beat your best score on it; re-checking a solved exercise adds nothing. Difficulty goes up (to at most 3) after a first-try pass without assistance, and down (to 1) after repeated failures. Beta builds are on the Releases page . Download the installer for your computer: The app bundles Codemm, so you don't need Node.js, npm or a terminal. The public 1.0 will be signed. Installing Docker Desktop needs admin rights, which school and work computers often don't give. Without Docker, the desktop app can still run io practice (programs that read input and print output) in interpreted languages that have a WebAssembly (WASI) build, such as Python. It bundles wasmtime , a sandbox that runs as your own user, with no admin rights. In Check this computer, choose Continue without Docker . For everything else, such as unit tests, frameworks and compiled languages, ask whoever manages the computer to install Docker Desktop once ( Docker's terms list education among free uses), or use a computer that has Docker. Codemm also works directly from your agent in a terminal. This needs Node.js 22 or newer and Docker (or wasmtime 50 on PATH , for the practice above), and installs from source (Codemm isn't on npm): This sets up Claude Code, Codex and Cursor; use --host claude (repeatable) to pick specific ones. It adds an MCP server entry for each agent, a Codemm section in AGENTS.md , an author subagent and the Claude Code practice hook. Existing config is merged, never replaced.
